section_summary: This closing section consists chiefly of Federal Communications Commission cover letters and monitored Morse transmissions from Jakarta Radio station PMC, repeatedly announcing an “American Hour” of news and revelations for listeners in the United States. It also contains a lengthy American Embassy report translating more than two hundred intercepted Japanese commercial, shipping, personnel, diplomatic-welfare, and private messages exchanged across East and Southeast Asia, together with a State Department forwarding note. A separate broadcast-intelligence report summarizes Japanese commentary on the anticipated battle for the Philippines, José P. Laurel’s opposition to Filipino conscription, and Akiyoshi Tajiri’s explanation of Philippine martial law.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC warning transmission to the United States
subfiles.about: A monitored Morse transmission announces Jakarta Radio's American program and urges United States listeners to receive its forthcoming news.
subfiles.summary: Station PMC identifies itself as broadcasting from Djakarta, Djawa, on 18,135 kilocycles. It says its American Hour will offer important news and revelations on international affairs that Americans supposedly cannot obtain elsewhere, and directs listeners to tune in by wireless telephony.

subfiles.title: FCC letter transmitting further Jakarta Radio intercepts
subfiles.from: G. E. Sterling, Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.to: Adolph A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: The FCC forwards additional intercepts of Jakarta Radio in response to Berle's request.
subfiles.summary: G. E. Sterling, Assistant Chief Engineer and Chief of the Radio Intelligence Division, sends the State Department further Jakarta Radio intercepts. The letter is marked confidential and lists enclosures.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC American Hour intercept
subfiles.about: An FCC monitoring station records PMC's standard appeal to American listeners.
subfiles.summary: The transmission gives PMC's frequency as 18,135 kilocycles and announces a program beginning at 1800 Pacific War Time. It promises important international news and directs Americans to listen to the Jakarta Broadcasting Station; the monitor notes severe fading but good hand keying.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC intercept of 23 August 1944
subfiles.about: The monitored transmission repeats Jakarta Radio's promotional warning for its American program.
subfiles.summary: PMC calls the United States and claims its coming program will supply vital news and revelations unavailable through American sources. The monitoring form describes heavy static, poor hand sending, and a blind transmission to call sign KAIA.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC intercept of 25 August 1944
subfiles.about: PMC broadcasts its recurring announcement of an American Hour from Jakarta.
subfiles.summary: The message identifies the frequency and promises an hour of international news for Americans beginning at 1800 Pacific War Time. It ends by announcing another transmission at 1135 Tokyo time; the monitor reports light static and fair hand keying.

subfiles.title: FCC letter transmitting further Jakarta Radio intercepts
subfiles.from: G. E. Sterling, Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.to: Adolph A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: The FCC sends Berle another group of Jakarta Radio intercepts.
subfiles.summary: The confidential registered letter responds to Berle's standing request for monitored Jakarta Radio traffic. Sterling signs as head of the FCC Radio Intelligence Division and notes that enclosures accompany the letter.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC American Hour intercept
subfiles.about: A monitored transmission urges Americans to listen to Jakarta Radio's promised international-affairs revelations.
subfiles.summary: PMC gives its wavelength and announces the American program for 1800 Pacific War Time. The standard warning says the coming broadcast will contain important information unavailable in the United States and announces another transmission at 1135 Tokyo time.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC American Hour intercept
subfiles.about: The intercept records PMC's recurring invitation to the United States audience.
subfiles.summary: The hand-sent message identifies Jakarta Radio and its 18,135-kilocycle frequency. It promises vital news and revelations, tells Americans they will profit from listening, and schedules the next call for 1135 Tokyo time.

subfiles.title: Incomplete Jakarta Radio PMC intercept
subfiles.about: An interrupted transmission begins PMC's standard American Hour announcement but goes off the air during the text.
subfiles.summary: PMC starts to identify the Jakarta station, its frequency, and the purpose of its American program. The signal pauses during the statement about international revelations and then goes off before the message is completed.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC American Hour intercept
subfiles.about: The complete monitored warning promotes Jakarta Radio's broadcasts to America.
subfiles.summary: PMC announces its wavelength as 18,135 kilocycles and says its program will begin at 1800 Pacific War Time. The transmission promises news unavailable elsewhere, urges Americans to listen, and says it will return at the same time the following day.

subfiles.title: FCC letter transmitting further Jakarta Radio intercepts
subfiles.from: G. E. Sterling, Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.to: Adolph A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: Sterling forwards another set of Jakarta Radio intercepts to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: The confidential letter states that the material is sent in accordance with Berle's request. Sterling identifies himself as Assistant Chief Engineer and Chief of the FCC Radio Intelligence Division.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC intercept of 7 September 1944
subfiles.about: PMC delivers its standard American Hour promotion and announces a subsequent Tokyo-time transmission.
subfiles.summary: The station promises important news and revelations bearing on international affairs and claims Americans cannot obtain them otherwise. It gives the operating frequency as 18,135 kilocycles and says the next transmission will be at 1135 Tokyo time.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC intercept of 8 September 1944
subfiles.about: An FCC monitor records a fading, partially garbled version of PMC's standard appeal.
subfiles.summary: Despite missing words, the transmission identifies Jakarta, gives the station's frequency, and promises vital international news to American listeners. It concludes by urging reception of the wireless-telephone program and announcing another transmission around 1130 Tokyo time.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC American Hour intercept
subfiles.about: PMC repeats its regular announcement for the American program over a poorly sent signal.
subfiles.summary: The station states that its program begins at 1800 Pacific War Time and will contain significant international news and revelations. It invites the United States audience to listen and schedules the next broadcast for 1135 Tokyo time.

subfiles.title: FCC letter transmitting further Jakarta Radio intercepts
subfiles.from: G. E. Sterling, Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.to: Adolph A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: The FCC forwards additional Jakarta Radio monitoring material.
subfiles.summary: Sterling sends the confidential enclosures by registered mail in response to Berle's request. The letter bears the State Department decimal-file reference for wireless broadcasting.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC American Hour intercept
subfiles.about: The monitored message advertises Jakarta Radio's American broadcast and its purported exclusive news.
subfiles.summary: PMC states its frequency as 18,135 kilocycles and announces the program for 1800 Pacific War Time. It claims the broadcast will contain vital revelations, urges Americans to listen, and gives the next transmission as 1135 Tokyo time.

subfiles.title: FCC letter transmitting further Jakarta Radio intercepts
subfiles.from: G. E. Sterling, Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.to: Adolph A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: Sterling sends Berle further FCC intercepts of Jakarta Radio.
subfiles.summary: The registered confidential letter follows the standard FCC transmittal form used throughout the file. It identifies the enclosed material only as further Jakarta Radio intercepts.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC American Hour intercept
subfiles.about: PMC's promotional transmission is monitored with static but no interference.
subfiles.summary: The sender repeats portions after keying errors and says the American program will provide news and revelations unavailable elsewhere. It urges listening to Jakarta Radio and announces another transmission at approximately 1130 Tokyo time.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC American Hour intercept
subfiles.about: A poorly hand-sent PMC transmission repeats the station's warning to American listeners.
subfiles.summary: The message promises important international news, asks Americans to prepare for a wireless-telephone broadcast, and says they will profit from listening. It concludes by scheduling another transmission for about 1130.

subfiles.title: FCC letter transmitting further Jakarta Radio intercepts
subfiles.from: G. E. Sterling, Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.to: Adolph A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: The FCC provides another confidential Jakarta Radio intercept enclosure.
subfiles.summary: Sterling states that the enclosed intercept is supplied in accordance with Berle's request. The letter is filed under the State Department's wireless-broadcasting decimal designation.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC American Hour intercept
subfiles.about: The intercept records PMC's familiar appeal to American audiences.
subfiles.summary: The station announces 18,135 kilocycles, an 1800 Pacific War Time program, and forthcoming international news and revelations. It directs Americans to Jakarta's wireless-telephone program and gives the next call as 1130 Tokyo time.

subfiles.title: Voluntary Report No. 107 on intercepted Japanese messages
subfiles.about: The embassy introduces translations of Japanese commercial and miscellaneous messages intercepted between 1 August and 2 September 1944.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum refers to an earlier embassy report of 7 September and explains that the attached traffic was intercepted by an Allied monitoring unit and translated by the American-operated Translation Center. It states that the collection contains commercial and miscellaneous messages, while certain texts concerning Japanese coercive-service recruitment were omitted for separate handling.

subfiles.title: Translations of intercepted Japanese commercial and miscellaneous messages
subfiles.about: The enclosure translates more than two hundred intercepted messages exchanged among Japanese-controlled commercial, transport, banking, government, and private correspondents.
subfiles.summary: The messages range across Bangkok, Saigon, Shanghai, Tokyo, Hanoi, Canton, and other Asian centers and concern rice, pepper, beans, rubber, shipping, warehouses, insurance, remittances, staffing, and wartime shortages. Several report Thailand's 1944 cabinet and regency changes, while others carry Red Cross inquiries, internee news, death notifications, and family greetings. The compilation also reveals extensive coordination among Japanese trading houses, banks, transport associations, military authorities, and local branches under increasingly difficult wartime conditions. Many translations preserve the original cable numbers, languages, prices, quantities, and routing information.

subfiles.title: State Department transmittal of Voluntary Report No. 107
subfiles.about: The Secretary of State sends the Director of Censorship a copy of the Chungking embassy's report on intercepted Japanese commercial messages.
subfiles.summary: The brief confidential note presents the information in the hope that it will be useful to the censorship authorities. Its enclosure is identified as American Embassy Voluntary Report No. 107, dated 5 October 1944.

subfiles.title: Foreign Broadcast Intelligence daily report for 4 October 1944
subfiles.about: The report summarizes Japanese and Philippine broadcasts about naval strategy, Filipino conscription, and martial law.
subfiles.summary: Admiral Nobumasa Suetsugu predicts that continuing air battles rather than a single fleet engagement will decide the war and calls the Philippines the decisive Pacific battleground. President José P. Laurel again rejects compulsory Filipino combat service while demanding other assistance to Japanese forces. Japanese minister Akiyoshi Tajiri argues that Philippine martial law was a Filipino-created mechanism for cooperation rather than direct Japanese military administration.

subfiles.title: FCC letter transmitting further Jakarta Radio intercepts
subfiles.from: G. E. Sterling, Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.to: Adolph A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: Sterling forwards additional monitored Jakarta Radio transmissions.
subfiles.summary: The confidential registered letter uses the established formula for providing Berle with further intercepts. Sterling signs as chief of the FCC Radio Intelligence Division and notes the enclosed monitoring sheets.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC American Hour intercept
subfiles.about: A well-keyed PMC transmission promotes Jakarta Radio's American Hour.
subfiles.summary: The transmission announces 18,135 kilocycles and promises important international news to Americans at 1800 Pacific War Time. It claims the information is otherwise unavailable, urges listening by wireless telephony, and schedules another transmission at 1130.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC American Hour intercept
subfiles.about: PMC repeats its standard American-service announcement through moderate static and interference.
subfiles.summary: The station identifies Jakarta, Java, and its 18,135-kilocycle frequency before promising exclusive news and revelations. It tells Americans they will profit by listening and announces a further transmission at 1130.

subfiles.title: FCC letter transmitting further Jakarta Radio intercepts
subfiles.from: G. E. Sterling, Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.to: Adolph A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: The FCC sends another installment of Jakarta Radio intercepts to Berle.
subfiles.summary: The confidential letter states that the enclosed monitoring material is furnished in accordance with Berle's request. It is signed by Sterling for the Radio Intelligence Division.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC intercept of 5 October 1944
subfiles.about: PMC's American Hour announcement is copied despite heavy atmospheric noise.
subfiles.summary: The transmission repeats the familiar promise of important international news unavailable through other sources in the United States. It gives the operating frequency and directs listeners to Jakarta Radio, ending with a reference to 1130 Tokyo time.

subfiles.title: FCC letter transmitting further Jakarta Radio intercepts
subfiles.from: G. E. Sterling, Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.to: Adolph A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: Sterling forwards further Jakarta Radio intercepts under the 12 October file reference.
subfiles.summary: The FCC's confidential registered letter continues the regular series of transmittals to the State Department. It identifies the enclosures as additional intercepts of Jakarta Radio.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC intercept of 7 October 1944
subfiles.about: A poorly sent PMC transmission announces the American program and its claimed international revelations.
subfiles.summary: The operator makes several corrections while giving Jakarta Radio's identity, frequency, and 1800 Pacific War Time schedule. The station urges Americans to listen to news they allegedly cannot obtain elsewhere and gives a subsequent time of 1130.

subfiles.title: FCC letter transmitting further Jakarta Radio intercepts
subfiles.from: G. E. Sterling, Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.to: Adolph A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: The FCC transmits another set of Jakarta Radio monitoring records.
subfiles.summary: The confidential cover letter is addressed to Berle and signed by Sterling as head of the FCC Radio Intelligence Division. It contains the same standing explanation that the intercepts are supplied at Berle's request.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC American Hour intercept
subfiles.about: PMC broadcasts the standard American Hour warning through severe atmospheric noise.
subfiles.summary: The message identifies Jakarta Radio, 18,135 kilocycles, and an 1800 Pacific War Time start. It promises important revelations, directs Americans to receive the wireless-telephone program, and announces another transmission at 1130 Tokyo time.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC American Hour intercept
subfiles.about: A second monitoring sheet records PMC's recurring promotional message.
subfiles.summary: The good hand-keyed transmission promises vital international news to the United States and repeats the claim that it is unobtainable elsewhere. It urges listening to Jakarta Radio and closes with notice of a later transmission.

subfiles.title: FCC letter transmitting further Jakarta Radio intercepts
subfiles.from: G. E. Sterling, Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.to: Adolph A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: Sterling sends Berle the final group of Jakarta Radio intercepts in this file section.
subfiles.summary: The registered confidential letter identifies its enclosures as further intercepts supplied under Berle's request. It is dated 17 October and was received and filed by the State Department on 23 October.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC intercept of 14 October 1944
subfiles.about: PMC repeats its American Hour announcement after an initially unreadable mixture of code and music.
subfiles.summary: Once readable, the transmission identifies Jakarta Radio and its frequency and promises an hour of important international news at 1800 Pacific War Time. It urges Americans to receive the wireless-telephone broadcast and closes with a reference to 1130 Tokyo time.

subfiles.title: Jakarta Radio PMC intercept, final sheet
subfiles.about: The file ends with another monitored version of PMC's appeal to American listeners.
subfiles.summary: The fair hand-keyed transmission identifies Jakarta, Java, gives a garbled version of the usual 18,135-kilocycle frequency, and promises news and revelations on international affairs. It tells the United States audience to prepare for the wireless-telephone broadcast, but the transcription ends before the normal closing formula.
